draft.title: Context and argument
card: Context is the when, where and for whom of an argument. It includes the time, the place, the occasion and the audience.
A writer or speaker shapes the argument to fit its context. The same issue can be argued in very different ways for different audiences.
Audience affects tone, language and evidence. A talk to young students may use simple words and a friendly tone. A report for experts may use technical terms and data.
Context also affects how people react. An argument that suits one time or place may be ignored or rejected in another.
draft.remember: Ask when, where and for whom, then ask how that shaped the argument.

a.q: Why might a speaker use a different tone for a school assembly than for a council meeting on the same issue?
opts: The audience and occasion differ, so the speaker adapts
The issue changes completely between the two events
Speakers must use the same tone in every place
Formal audiences never respond to emotional appeals
a.why: Context includes the occasion and the audience, and a speaker shapes the argument to fit them. The issue can stay the same, so the second option is wrong, because the change comes from the context.
a.clue: Think about who is listening in each room.

b.q: Priya argues for a later school start. She first speaks to her Year 7 classmates, then writes to the school board. Which change best shows her adapting to context?
opts: She adds survey data and a formal tone for the board
She uses the same casual words in both places
She drops her main point for the board
She writes to the board in the same style as to friends
b.why: The board is a formal audience that expects evidence, so data and a formal tone fit that context. Using the same casual words ignores the change in audience, so it does not show adapting.
b.clue: Which audience would expect evidence and formal language?

a.best: The audience and occasion differ, so the speaker adapts

b.best: She adds survey data and a formal tone for the board

problems.detail: The clue 'Which audience would expect evidence and formal language?' almost restates the right option ('survey data and a formal tone'), so students can match words without understanding context.
The right option is the only one describing a positive change with a precise detail (survey data, formal tone). The others are all 'same' or 'drops', so it stands out without knowledge of the idea.
Two distractors use absolutes ('must use the same tone in every place', 'never respond'), which makes them easy to rule out on wording alone.
